questions.question: What is the 'split-brain' problem in distributed systems?

options.text: Two partitions each believing they are the authoritative cluster, potentially accepting conflicting writes

questions.explanation: Split-brain occurs during network partition when isolated groups each elect their own leader and accept writes independently. When partition heals, conflicting data must be reconciled—a serious consistency problem.

questions.question: How does quorum-based voting prevent split-brain?

options.text: Only the partition with majority of nodes can make decisions

questions.explanation: Quorum requires majority (N/2 + 1) agreement. During partition, only one side can have majority. The minority partition cannot achieve quorum and must stop accepting writes, preventing conflicting decisions.

questions.question: A 4-node cluster experiences a network partition splitting it 2-2. What is the problem?

options.text: Neither side has majority, so neither can make progress (or both might, causing split-brain)

questions.explanation: With even nodes, a 50-50 split has no majority. Neither side can achieve quorum. If the system doesn't handle this, both might operate independently (split-brain). This is why odd node counts are recommended.

questions.question: What is a 'witness' or 'arbiter' node in preventing split-brain?

options.text: A lightweight node that participates in voting but doesn't store data

questions.explanation: Witness/arbiter nodes participate in quorum voting without storing data. They break ties in even-node clusters. Example: 2 data nodes + 1 witness = 3 votes, enabling majority decisions.

questions.question: What is STONITH and how does it prevent split-brain?

options.text: 'Shoot The Other Node In The Head' - forcibly shutting down nodes to ensure only one partition operates

questions.explanation: STONITH (or fencing) forcibly powers off or isolates nodes that might cause split-brain. If a node is suspected of being in a minority partition, it's killed to ensure it can't accept writes.

questions.question: True or False: Split-brain can only occur with network partitions.
questions.explanation: Split-brain can also occur from: slow nodes appearing dead (false failure detection), misconfigured timeouts, or bugs in leader election. Any situation where multiple nodes believe they're the leader can cause split-brain.

questions.question: A database cluster uses leader-based replication. During split-brain, what is the worst-case scenario?

options.text: Two leaders accepting conflicting writes, causing data divergence

questions.explanation: Two leaders = two sources of truth. Both accept writes that conflict (e.g., different values for same key). When partition heals, data has diverged. Reconciliation may lose data or require manual intervention.

questions.question: How does ZooKeeper prevent split-brain in distributed systems?

options.text: Uses Zab consensus requiring majority quorum for all decisions

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper uses Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast) consensus. All writes require majority acknowledgment. During partition, minority cannot write. This makes ZooKeeper a reliable coordination service for leader election.

questions.question: What is 'fencing' in the context of split-brain prevention?

options.text: Mechanisms to prevent a node from accessing shared resources after being considered failed

questions.explanation: Fencing ensures a 'dead' node can't access shared resources (storage, network). Methods: power fencing (cut power), storage fencing (revoke access), network fencing (block traffic). Prevents zombie nodes causing split-brain.

questions.question: A Kubernetes cluster loses connectivity to the control plane. What prevents split-brain in pod scheduling?

options.text: etcd's Raft consensus ensures only majority partition can schedule

questions.explanation: Kubernetes control plane uses etcd (Raft consensus). Only the partition with etcd majority can make scheduling decisions. Minority partition's control plane becomes read-only, preventing conflicting schedules.

questions.question: Which design choices help prevent split-brain? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: Odd nodes ensure clear majority. Quorum requires majority for decisions. Fencing kills potentially rogue nodes. Ignoring partitions guarantees split-brain when they occur.

questions.question: After split-brain is detected and resolved, what must happen to the data?

options.text: Conflicting writes must be identified and reconciled

questions.explanation: Split-brain may have caused conflicting writes. Reconciliation strategies: last-write-wins (may lose data), merge (if possible), manual resolution, or application-specific logic. This is why preventing split-brain is critical.
